title: Eiffel Tower
hints: A wrought-iron lattice tower finished in 1889
Built as the entrance arch to a World's Fair
Critics of the day called it a useless and monstrous eyesore
Locals nickname it 'the iron lady'
Stands on a long park called the Champ de Mars
Found in Paris, France
fact: At 330 m it was the tallest man-made structure on Earth for 41 years.

title: Forbidden City
hints: A walled palace complex with about 980 buildings
Home to emperors for nearly 500 years
Built between 1406 and 1420
Ordinary people were once barred from entering it
Sits just north of Tiananmen Square
Found in Beijing, China
fact: It now houses the Palace Museum, one of the most visited museums in the world.

title: The White House
hints: An official residence and workplace of a head of state
Every holder of the office has lived here since 1800
Burned by the British Army in 1814
Its most famous room is oval
The address is 1600 Pennsylvania Avenue
Found in Washington, D.C., USA
fact: It has 132 rooms, 35 bathrooms and 28 fireplaces.

title: Statue of Liberty
hints: A colossal copper statue that has turned green
A gift from the people of France in 1886
Designed by sculptor Bartholdi with an iron frame by Eiffel
She holds a torch and a tablet dated July 4, 1776
Stands on a small island in a harbor
Found in New York City, USA
fact: The seven rays of her crown represent the seven continents and seas.

title: Colosseum
hints: The largest ancient amphitheatre ever built
Could hold some 50,000 to 80,000 spectators
Completed in AD 80 under Emperor Titus
Hosted gladiator contests and staged sea battles
Officially named after the Flavian dynasty
Found in Rome, Italy
fact: Earthquakes and stone robbers removed about two-thirds of the original structure.

title: Taj Mahal
hints: An ivory-white marble mausoleum
Built by a Mughal emperor for his favorite wife
Construction began in 1632 and took about 20 years
Its marble changes color with the light of day
Sits on the bank of the Yamuna River
Found in Agra, India
fact: Around 20,000 artisans worked on it, and some 1,000 elephants hauled materials.

title: Machu Picchu
hints: A 15th-century citadel high in the mountains
Built by the Inca and abandoned a century later
Brought to world attention by Hiram Bingham in 1911
Famous for dry-stone walls fitted without mortar
Sits at about 2,430 m above sea level in the Andes
Found in the Cusco Region of Peru
fact: The Spanish never found it, which is why it survived largely intact.

title: Great Pyramid of Giza
hints: The oldest of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World
The only one still largely intact
Built as a tomb for the pharaoh Khufu around 2560 BC
Made of about 2.3 million stone blocks
A giant sphinx stands guard nearby
Found on the Giza plateau outside Cairo, Egypt
fact: It was the tallest human-made structure for more than 3,800 years.

title: Christ the Redeemer
hints: A 30 m Art Deco statue on a mountain top
Completed in 1931 and made of reinforced concrete and soapstone
Its arms stretch 28 m wide
Stands on the summit of Mount Corcovado
Overlooks a famous beach city and Sugarloaf Mountain
Found in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil
fact: Lightning strikes the statue several times a year and once chipped a thumb.

title: Sydney Opera House
hints: A performing arts centre with sail-shaped shells
Designed by Danish architect Jørn Utzon
Opened in 1973, ten years late and 14 times over budget
More than a million roof tiles cover it
Sits on Bennelong Point beside a famous harbour bridge
Found in Sydney, Australia
fact: Utzon left the project in 1966 and never returned to see it finished.

title: Big Ben
hints: A clock tower at the end of a parliament building
The nickname refers to the great bell inside
Officially renamed the Elizabeth Tower in 2012
Its four clock faces are each 7 m across
Stands beside the River Thames
Found in London, England
fact: The tower leans about 0.26 degrees, visible to the naked eye from some angles.

title: Golden Gate Bridge
hints: A suspension bridge painted 'International Orange'
Opened in 1937 across a strait
Was the longest main span in the world for 27 years
Frequently wrapped in fog
Connects a famous city to Marin County
Found in San Francisco, USA
fact: The color was originally just a primer; the architect liked it and kept it.

title: Acropolis of Athens
hints: An ancient citadel on a rocky outcrop above a capital
Its most famous building is a temple to a virgin goddess
Most of the monuments date to the 5th century BC
Lord Elgin removed many of its marbles in the 1800s
The temple is the Parthenon
Found in Athens, Greece
fact: The Parthenon served as a church, a mosque, and a gunpowder store before becoming a ruin.

title: Petra
hints: An ancient city carved into rose-red sandstone cliffs
Capital of the Nabataean kingdom around the 4th century BC
Reached through a narrow gorge called the Siq
Its most famous facade is 'The Treasury'
Featured in Indiana Jones and the Last Crusade
Found in southern Jordan
fact: Rediscovered for the Western world by Swiss explorer Johann Burckhardt in 1812.

title: Angkor Wat
hints: The largest religious monument in the world
Built in the early 12th century as a Hindu temple
Later converted to a Buddhist temple
Surrounded by a moat and appears on a national flag
Near the town of Siem Reap
Found in Cambodia
fact: Its five towers represent the peaks of Mount Meru, home of the gods.

title: Chichén Itzá
hints: A pre-Columbian city built by the Maya
Its step pyramid is called El Castillo
At the equinox a shadow serpent slithers down its stairs
Has a great ball court 168 m long
Lies on the Yucatán Peninsula
Found in Mexico
fact: Clap at the base of the pyramid and the echo sounds like the chirp of a quetzal bird.

title: Great Wall at Badaling
hints: The most visited section of a very long wall
Built to protect against nomadic raids from the north
Most of the surviving stone wall dates from the Ming dynasty
Contrary to legend, it is not visible from space with the naked eye
About 80 km northwest of a capital city
Found near Beijing, China
fact: All branches of the wall together run more than 21,000 km.

title: Stonehenge
hints: A prehistoric ring of standing stones
Built in stages from about 3000 BC
Aligned with the sunrise on the summer solstice
Some of its bluestones came from Wales, 250 km away
Stands on Salisbury Plain
Found in Wiltshire, England
fact: Each of the large sarsen stones weighs about 25 tonnes.

title: Neuschwanstein Castle
hints: A 19th-century hilltop castle built for a 'mad' king
Commissioned by Ludwig II of Bavaria in 1869
He lived there only 172 days before his mysterious death
Inspired the Sleeping Beauty castle at Disneyland
Sits above the village of Hohenschwangau in the Alps
Found in Bavaria, Germany
fact: Ludwig built it as a private refuge; it opened to paying visitors seven weeks after he died.

title: Sagrada Família
hints: A basilica under construction since 1882
Designed by architect Antoni Gaudí
Gaudí is buried in its crypt
When finished it will have 18 spires
Its nativity and passion facades are strikingly different
Found in Barcelona, Spain
fact: Gaudí said 'My client is not in a hurry' when asked about the building timeline.

title: Burj Khalifa
hints: The tallest building in the world since 2009
Rises 828 m with more than 160 floors
Its design is based on a desert flower
Stands beside the world's largest dancing fountain
Was renamed for a neighboring emirate's ruler at opening
Found in Dubai, UAE
fact: Residents on the top floors see the sun set a few minutes later than those at ground level.

title: Mount Rushmore
hints: Four 18 m heads carved into a granite mountain
Sculptor Gutzon Borglum worked on it from 1927 to 1941
The faces are Washington, Jefferson, Roosevelt, and Lincoln
Behind the heads is an unfinished 'Hall of Records'
Located in the Black Hills
Found in South Dakota, USA
fact: About 90% of the carving was done with dynamite.

title: Hagia Sophia
hints: A domed building that has been a church, a mosque, a museum, and a mosque again
Completed in 537 under Emperor Justinian
Was the largest cathedral in the world for nearly 1,000 years
Its name means 'Holy Wisdom'
Stands across from the Blue Mosque
Found in Istanbul, Turkey
fact: Its central dome is 31 m across and seems to float on a ring of 40 windows.

title: Moai of Easter Island
hints: Nearly 900 giant stone heads on a remote island
Carved by the Rapa Nui people between 1250 and 1500
Most were quarried at the volcano Rano Raraku
Many have full bodies buried beneath the ground
One of the most isolated inhabited islands on Earth
Found on Easter Island, Chile
fact: The largest statue ever moved weighs 82 tonnes; one left unfinished in the quarry would weigh 270.

title: Leaning Tower of Pisa
hints: A freestanding bell tower that famously tilts
Began leaning during construction in the 12th century because of soft ground
Took 199 years to complete
Engineers reduced the lean by 45 cm in the 1990s
Stands in the Piazza dei Miracoli
Found in Pisa, Italy
fact: Galileo is said to have dropped cannonballs from it to test gravity.

title: Alhambra
hints: A palace and fortress complex on a hill
Built mostly by the Nasrid dynasty in the 13th and 14th centuries
Famous for its intricate Islamic plasterwork and courtyards
Its name means 'the red one' in Arabic
Overlooks a city in Andalusia
Found in Granada, Spain
fact: The Court of the Lions fountain once worked as a water clock.

title: Moscow Kremlin
hints: A fortified complex that is the seat of a national government
Its red brick walls were built in the 1480s by Italian architects
Contains cathedrals, palaces, and the world's largest bell
Faces an onion-domed cathedral across a famous square
That square is called Red Square
Found in Moscow, Russia
fact: The Tsar Bell, at 202 tonnes, cracked before it was ever rung.

title: Brandenburg Gate
hints: An 18th-century neoclassical city gate
Topped by a four-horse chariot driven by the goddess of victory
Napoleon took the chariot to Paris in 1806
Stood just inside a dividing wall from 1961 to 1989
At the end of the boulevard Unter den Linden
Found in Berlin, Germany
fact: Ronald Reagan said 'tear down this wall' from a podium just in front of it.

title: Tower Bridge
hints: A bascule and suspension bridge opened in 1894
Its two towers are linked by high-level walkways
The road deck lifts about 800 times a year
Often mistaken for a plainer bridge upstream
Named for a nearby medieval fortress
Found in London, England
fact: In 1952 a bus had to jump the gap when the bridge began to open with it still on the deck.

title: Palace of Versailles
hints: A royal palace that began as a hunting lodge
Louis XIV moved his court here in 1682
Has a 73 m Hall of Mirrors
The treaty ending the First World War was signed here
About 20 km southwest of a capital
Found near Paris, France
fact: The gardens contain more than 50 fountains and 600 jets of water.

title: The Louvre
hints: The most visited museum in the world
Began as a 12th-century fortress, then a royal palace
Its glass pyramid entrance opened in 1989
Home to the Venus de Milo and the Winged Victory
Also home to a small, smiling portrait by Leonardo
Found in Paris, France
fact: Seeing every piece for 30 seconds each would take about 100 days.

title: Blue Mosque
hints: A 17th-century mosque with six minarets
Named for the blue İznik tiles inside
Officially called the Sultan Ahmed Mosque
Six minarets caused a scandal, matching Mecca at the time
Faces an ancient domed basilica across a park
Found in Istanbul, Turkey
fact: More than 20,000 handmade ceramic tiles decorate its interior.

title: CN Tower
hints: A 553 m concrete communications and observation tower
The tallest free-standing structure in the world from 1976 to 2007
Has a glass floor 342 m up
Visitors can walk hands-free around the outside edge
Beside a domed baseball stadium
Found in Toronto, Canada
fact: The 'CN' stands for Canadian National, the railway that built it.

title: Space Needle
hints: A 184 m observation tower with a flying-saucer top
Built for the 1962 World's Fair
Designed to withstand 9.0 earthquakes and 320 km/h winds
Its colors at opening included 'Galaxy Gold' and 'Orbital Olive'
In a rainy Pacific Northwest city
Found in Seattle, USA
fact: Its elevators slow down in high winds, taking a leisurely ride to the top.

title: Gateway Arch
hints: A 192 m stainless steel arch
The tallest man-made monument in the Western Hemisphere
Designed by Eero Saarinen and completed in 1965
Commemorates westward expansion of the United States
Stands on the bank of the Mississippi River
Found in St. Louis, USA
fact: It is exactly as wide as it is tall: 630 feet.

title: Hollywood Sign
hints: Nine white letters, each 14 m tall, on a hillside
Erected in 1923 as an advertisement for a housing development
Originally read 'Hollywoodland'
Restored in 1978 with donations from celebrities
Overlooks the film capital of the world
Found in Los Angeles, USA
fact: Hugh Hefner bought the letter Y in the 1978 fundraiser; Alice Cooper bought an O.

title: Alcatraz Island
hints: A small island prison that closed in 1963
Housed Al Capone and 'the Birdman'
No confirmed escape ever succeeded
Occupied by Native American activists from 1969 to 1971
Sits in a bay near an orange bridge
Found in San Francisco Bay, USA
fact: The name comes from the Spanish for 'pelicans'.

title: Potala Palace
hints: A 13-storey fortress-palace on a mountainside
Winter residence of the Dalai Lamas from 1649 to 1959
Contains over 1,000 rooms and 200,000 statues
Stands at about 3,700 m above sea level
Overlooks a city on the Tibetan Plateau
Found in Lhasa, Tibet
fact: Its walls are up to 5 m thick and were strengthened with molten copper against earthquakes.

title: Borobudur
hints: The world's largest Buddhist temple
Built in the 9th century and later abandoned beneath volcanic ash
Has 504 Buddha statues and 2,672 relief panels
Shaped like a giant stepped mandala
On the island of Java
Found in Indonesia
fact: Pilgrims walk clockwise up its nine levels, a path of about 5 km.

title: Himeji Castle
hints: A hilltop castle with brilliant white plaster walls
Nicknamed the 'White Heron Castle'
Survived WWII bombing and the 1995 Kobe earthquake
Its present form dates from 1609
Considered the finest surviving example of its country's castle architecture
Found in Hyōgo Prefecture, Japan
fact: A firebomb landed on the top floor during the war but failed to explode.

title: Fushimi Inari Shrine
hints: A shrine famous for thousands of vermilion gates
Each gate was donated by a business
Dedicated to the god of rice and foxes
The trails climb a 233 m sacred mountain
In the former imperial capital of its country
Found in Kyoto, Japan
fact: There are about 10,000 torii gates along the trails.

title: Petronas Towers
hints: Twin skyscrapers joined by a sky bridge
The tallest buildings in the world from 1998 to 2004
Floor plans are based on an eight-pointed Islamic star
Named for a national oil company
In a Southeast Asian capital
Found in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia
fact: Each tower was built by a different contractor racing the other.

title: Marina Bay Sands
hints: Three hotel towers topped by a ship-shaped sky park
Opened in 2010 and has a 150 m rooftop infinity pool
Designed by architect Moshe Safdie
Faces a lion-fish statue across the water
In a city-state at the tip of a peninsula
Found in Singapore
fact: The SkyPark cantilevers 67 m beyond the towers, one of the longest in the world.

title: Wat Arun
hints: A riverside temple with a tall porcelain-covered spire
Known as the Temple of Dawn
Its central prang is decorated with broken Chinese porcelain
Stands on the west bank of the Chao Phraya River
Across from the Grand Palace
Found in Bangkok, Thailand
fact: It is named after Aruna, the Hindu god of dawn.

title: Sheikh Zayed Grand Mosque
hints: A white marble mosque with 82 domes
Completed in 2007 and holds 40,000 worshippers
Contains the world's largest hand-knotted carpet
Its chandeliers are studded with Swarovski crystals
Named for the founding father of its country
Found in Abu Dhabi, UAE
fact: The carpet weighs 35 tonnes and took 1,200 artisans two years to make.

title: Table Mountain
hints: A flat-topped mountain that looms over a port city
A cable car has run to the top since 1929
Often draped in a cloud 'tablecloth'
Home to more plant species than the whole of Britain
One of the New7Wonders of Nature
Found in Cape Town, South Africa
fact: It is one of the oldest mountains on Earth, around 260 million years old.

title: Pyramid of the Sun, Teotihuacan
hints: The third-largest pyramid in the world
Built around AD 200 by a culture whose name is unknown
Aligned along a broad 'Avenue of the Dead'
The Aztecs later named the city 'place where gods were born'
About 40 km northeast of a huge capital
Found near Mexico City, Mexico
fact: At its peak the city held perhaps 125,000 people, among the largest in the world.

title: Hoover Dam
hints: A 221 m concrete arch-gravity dam completed in 1936
Built during the Great Depression by thousands of workers
Created the largest reservoir in the United States
Straddles the border of two states and two time zones
On the Colorado River in Black Canyon
Found between Nevada and Arizona, USA
fact: The concrete is still curing and generating heat decades after it was poured.

title: Panama Canal (Miraflores Locks)
hints: A set of locks on a famous ship canal
The canal opened in 1914 and joins two oceans
Ships are lifted 26 m to a man-made lake
Expanded with wider locks in 2016
On the Pacific end of the waterway
Found in Panama
fact: Because of the isthmus's curve, ships travel from the Atlantic to the Pacific heading southeast.

title: Meteora
hints: Monasteries perched on top of giant sandstone pillars
Monks first climbed the rocks in the 11th century
Six of the original 24 monasteries are still active
Supplies were once hauled up in nets and baskets
The name means 'suspended in the air'
Found in Thessaly, Greece
fact: A James Bond villain's lair was filmed here in 'For Your Eyes Only'.

title: Tokyo
hints: The most populous metropolitan area in the world
Formerly called Edo
Became the capital in 1868
Home to the world's busiest pedestrian crossing
Hosted the Summer Olympics in 1964 and 2021
The capital of Japan
fact: Its Tsukiji and Toyosu fish markets have handled single tuna sold for over $3 million.

title: New York City
hints: A city of five boroughs
Bought from Native Americans for goods worth about 60 guilders, legend says
Originally named New Amsterdam
Home to the United Nations headquarters
Nicknamed the Big Apple
The largest city in the USA
fact: More than 800 languages are spoken here, the most of any city on Earth.

title: London
hints: Founded by the Romans as Londinium
Rebuilt after a great fire in 1666
Has the world's oldest underground railway
Hosted the Summer Olympics three times
Straddles the River Thames
The capital of the United Kingdom
fact: The 'Big Smoke' had smogs so thick in 1952 that one killed an estimated 12,000 people.

title: Paris
hints: Nicknamed the City of Light
Its 20 districts spiral outward like a snail shell
Rebuilt with wide boulevards by Baron Haussmann in the 1800s
Home to the most visited museum in the world
Built around an island in the Seine
The capital of France
fact: There is only one stop sign in the entire city.

title: Cairo
hints: The largest city in Africa and the Arab world
Founded in AD 969 by the Fatimid dynasty
Nicknamed the City of a Thousand Minarets
Ancient pyramids stand on its western edge
Sits on the Nile just upstream of its delta
The capital of Egypt
fact: Its name in Arabic, al-Qāhirah, means 'the Vanquisher'.

title: Rio de Janeiro
hints: Famous for a giant carnival and a giant statue
Portuguese explorers mistook its bay for a river mouth in January 1502
Was a national capital until 1960
Home to Copacabana and Ipanema beaches
Hosted the 2016 Summer Olympics
The second-largest city in Brazil
fact: Its name means 'River of January' even though there is no river.

title: Sydney
hints: Founded in 1788 as a British penal colony
Its harbour is one of the largest natural harbours in the world
Home to Bondi Beach
Hosted the 2000 Summer Olympics
Often mistaken for its country's capital
The largest city in Australia
fact: Its harbour bridge is nicknamed 'the Coathanger'.

title: Istanbul
hints: The only major city on two continents
Formerly Byzantium, then Constantinople
Capital of the Roman, Byzantine, and Ottoman empires
Its Grand Bazaar has more than 4,000 shops
Split by a strait called the Bosphorus
The largest city in Turkey
fact: Despite its size, it is not the capital; that is Ankara.

title: Mumbai
hints: Built on seven islands joined by land reclamation
Formerly called Bombay
Home to the Bollywood film industry
Its 'dabbawalas' deliver 200,000 lunchboxes a day
On the Arabian Sea coast
The largest city in India
fact: A single home here, Antilia, is 27 storeys tall and valued at over $1 billion.

title: Mexico City
hints: Built on the ruins of the Aztec capital Tenochtitlan
Stands on a drained lake bed and is sinking up to 50 cm a year
At 2,240 m, one of the highest major cities
Hosted the 1968 Summer Olympics
Home to the largest cathedral in the Americas
The capital of Mexico
fact: The Aztecs founded it where they saw an eagle eating a snake on a cactus, now the national emblem.

title: Moscow
hints: The most populous city entirely in Europe
Its metro stations are famous for chandeliers and mosaics
Napoleon occupied it in 1812 and found it on fire
Has more billionaires than almost any other city
Home to a famous fortress and onion-domed cathedral
The capital of Russia
fact: Its metro carries more than 6 million passengers a day.

title: Beijing
hints: A capital for most of the last 800 years
Its name means 'Northern Capital'
The only city to host both Summer and Winter Olympics
Home to the largest public square in the world
Its old centre is a grid of hutong alleys
The capital of China
fact: Its historic centre was laid out on a north-south axis nearly 8 km long.

title: Buenos Aires
hints: The birthplace of tango
Its name means 'fair winds'
Has the widest avenue in the world, 9 de Julio
Home to a famous cemetery where Eva Perón is buried
On the Río de la Plata estuary
The capital of Argentina
fact: It has more bookshops per person than any other city in the world.

title: Cape Town
hints: Founded in 1652 as a supply station for Dutch ships
Nelson Mandela was imprisoned on an island in its bay
Overlooked by a flat-topped mountain
Its Bo-Kaap district is famous for brightly painted houses
One of three national capitals
The legislative capital of South Africa
fact: Robben Island's name comes from the Dutch word for seals.

title: Singapore
hints: A city-state founded as a trading post by Stamford Raffles in 1819
Expelled from a neighboring federation in 1965
Chewing gum sales have been banned since 1992
Has one of the busiest ports in the world
Lies just 137 km north of the equator
An island nation at the tip of the Malay Peninsula
fact: Its name means 'Lion City', though lions have never lived there.

title: Hong Kong
hints: A former British colony handed over in 1997
Has more skyscrapers than any other city
Its name means 'fragrant harbour'
Famous for a tram up to Victoria Peak
Its Star Ferry has crossed the harbour since 1888
A special administrative region of China
fact: Its airport was built on an island made by flattening two existing islands.

title: Dubai
hints: A desert city that was a pearl-diving village a century ago
Home to the world's tallest building
Built artificial islands shaped like palm trees
Has an indoor ski slope in a shopping mall
On the Persian Gulf
The largest city in the United Arab Emirates
fact: Only about 15% of its residents are citizens of the country.

title: Rome
hints: Legend says it was founded in 753 BC by twins raised by a wolf
Known as the Eternal City
Contains an entire sovereign state within its borders
Has more than 2,000 fountains
Built on seven hills beside the Tiber
The capital of Italy
fact: About 3,000 euros a day are thrown into the Trevi Fountain and donated to charity.

title: Bangkok
hints: Its full ceremonial name is 168 letters long
Known for tuk-tuks and floating markets
Was once called the Venice of the East for its canals
Among the most visited cities in the world
On the Chao Phraya River
The capital of Thailand
fact: Locals call it Krung Thep, 'City of Angels'.

title: Nairobi
hints: Began in 1899 as a railway depot
Its name comes from a Maasai phrase meaning 'cool water'
The only capital with a national park inside its borders
Home to the UN Environment Programme headquarters
Nicknamed the Green City in the Sun
The capital of Kenya
fact: Lions and giraffes roam a park just 7 km from downtown skyscrapers.

title: Reykjavík
hints: The world's northernmost capital city
Heated almost entirely by geothermal energy
Its name means 'smoky bay' after steam from hot springs
Has a hilltop church shaped like basalt columns
Reagan and Gorbachev held a summit here in 1986
The capital of Iceland
fact: Nearly two-thirds of the country's population lives in its metro area.

title: Venice
hints: A city built on 118 small islands
Has about 400 bridges and no cars
Famous for gondolas and a February carnival of masks
Was a powerful maritime republic for a thousand years
Its main square is named for St. Mark
Found in northeastern Italy
fact: The city rests on millions of wooden piles driven into mud centuries ago.

title: Jerusalem
hints: A holy city for three major religions
Its Old City is divided into four quarters
Destroyed and rebuilt at least twice in antiquity
Home to the Western Wall and the Dome of the Rock
Sits in the Judaean Mountains
Found between the Mediterranean and the Dead Sea
fact: 'Jerusalem syndrome' is a documented condition in which visitors believe they are biblical figures.

title: Havana
hints: Famous for vintage American cars and cigars
Founded by the Spanish in 1519
Hemingway lived nearby for 20 years
Its seafront promenade is called the Malecón
On the north coast of a Caribbean island
The capital of Cuba
fact: The classic cars survive because a 1960s import ban left owners nothing newer to buy.

title: Marrakech
hints: Known as the Red City for its sandstone walls
Founded in 1070 by the Almoravids
Its main square fills with snake charmers and food stalls at night
That square is Jemaa el-Fnaa
Sits at the foot of the Atlas Mountains
Found in Morocco
fact: The country's name in several languages comes from the name of this city.

title: San Francisco
hints: Boomed during the 1849 Gold Rush
Destroyed by earthquake and fire in 1906
Famous for cable cars and steep streets
Has the crookedest street in the world
Home to an orange suspension bridge
Found in northern California, USA
fact: Its summer fog has an official name: Karl.

title: Chicago
hints: Rebuilt after a great fire in 1871, reputedly started by a cow
Birthplace of the skyscraper
Reversed the flow of its river in 1900
Dyes that river green every St. Patrick's Day
Nicknamed the Windy City
On the shore of Lake Michigan, USA
fact: Its deep-dish pizza is eaten with a knife and fork.

title: New Orleans
hints: Birthplace of jazz
Famous for Mardi Gras and beignets
Sold to the United States by France in 1803
Much of the city lies below sea level
Its oldest neighborhood is the French Quarter
Near the mouth of the Mississippi River, USA
fact: Above-ground tombs are used because the water table is too high to bury the dead.

title: Vancouver
hints: A Pacific port backed by snow-capped mountains
Hosted the 2010 Winter Olympics
Has a 400-hectare park larger than Central Park
Nicknamed Hollywood North for its film industry
Consistently ranked among the most livable cities
Found in British Columbia, Canada
fact: You can ski and sail on the same day for much of the year.

title: Lima
hints: Founded by Francisco Pizarro in 1535 as the City of Kings
The second-largest desert city in the world after Cairo
Almost never rains, but is cloudy half the year
Famous for ceviche and pisco sours
On the Pacific coast of South America
The capital of Peru
fact: Its central district is a UNESCO site for its colonial balconies.

title: Seoul
hints: A capital for over 600 years
Lies just 50 km from a heavily fortified border
Hosted the 1988 Summer Olympics
Has the fastest average internet in the world
Split by the Han River
The capital of South Korea
fact: Its metropolitan area holds about half the country's population.

title: Amsterdam
hints: A city of canals, bicycles, and narrow houses
Named for a dam on the river Amstel
Houses lean forward on purpose to hoist furniture
Home to Anne Frank's hiding place
Has more bicycles than people
The capital of the Netherlands
fact: Around 15,000 bicycles are fished out of its canals every year.

title: Prague
hints: Known as the City of a Hundred Spires
Has a 600-year-old astronomical clock
Its castle is the largest ancient castle complex in the world
Two defenestrations here started wars
Spanned by the medieval Charles Bridge over the Vltava
The capital of the Czech Republic
fact: Its citizens drink more beer per capita than any other nation.

title: Athens
hints: One of the oldest cities in the world, inhabited for 5,000 years
Birthplace of democracy
Hosted the first modern Olympics in 1896
Named after a goddess who gifted it an olive tree
Dominated by a rocky hill with ancient temples
The capital of Greece
fact: Its ancient marathon route is still run every November.

title: Edinburgh
hints: Built on extinct volcanoes
Hosts the largest arts festival in the world every August
Its castle sits atop a volcanic plug
Harry Potter was partly written in its cafés
Nicknamed Auld Reekie
The capital of Scotland
fact: A one o'clock gun has fired from the castle almost every day since 1861.

title: Kyoto
hints: An imperial capital for more than 1,000 years
Has about 1,600 Buddhist temples and 400 Shinto shrines
Spared from atomic bombing on the order of a US secretary of war
Famous for geisha in the Gion district
Gave its name to a 1997 climate treaty
Found on Honshu, Japan
fact: Nintendo was founded here in 1889 as a playing-card company.

title: Hanoi
hints: Celebrated its 1,000th birthday in 2010
Its Old Quarter has 36 streets each once named for a trade
Trains squeeze through a street between houses
Home to a lake with a legendary sword-stealing turtle
Its name means 'inside the rivers'
The capital of Vietnam
fact: Egg coffee, made with whipped yolk, was invented here during a 1940s milk shortage.

title: Lagos
hints: One of the fastest-growing megacities on Earth
Was its country's capital until 1991
Centre of the Nollywood film industry
Named by the Portuguese after a town in the Algarve
Spreads across islands and a lagoon
The largest city in Nigeria
fact: Nollywood produces around 2,500 films a year, second only to Bollywood.

title: Honolulu
hints: The most remote major city in the world
Home to Waikiki Beach and an extinct volcano called Diamond Head
A nearby naval base was attacked in December 1941
Birthplace of a US president
Its name means 'sheltered harbor'
The capital of Hawaii
fact: It is the only US state capital with a royal palace.

title: Wellington
hints: The southernmost capital city in the world
Windier on average than Chicago
Home to a famous film studio where Lord of the Rings was made
Its red cable car climbs to a botanic garden
At the southern tip of its country's North Island
The capital of New Zealand
fact: It has more cafés and restaurants per head than New York City.

title: Grand Canyon
hints: A gorge 446 km long and up to 1.8 km deep
Carved by a river over about 6 million years
Its rocks at the bottom are nearly 2 billion years old
Teddy Roosevelt called it the one great sight every American should see
Cut by the Colorado River
Found in Arizona, USA

title: Mount Everest
hints: The highest point on Earth above sea level
Known locally as Sagarmatha and Chomolungma
First summited in 1953 by Hillary and Tenzing
Grows about 4 mm taller each year
Lies in the Himalayas on an international border
Found between Nepal and Tibet
fact: Its summit rock is marine limestone, once the floor of an ancient sea.

title: Niagara Falls
hints: Three waterfalls with the highest flow rate in North America
Daredevils have gone over in barrels since 1901
Was switched off in 1969 to study erosion
Straddles an international border
Between Lake Erie and Lake Ontario
Found on the USA-Canada border
fact: The falls have retreated about 11 km upstream in 12,000 years.

title: Uluru
hints: A giant sandstone monolith in a desert
Sacred to the Anangu people
Glows red at sunrise and sunset
Climbing it was banned in 2019
Also called Ayers Rock
Found in the Northern Territory, Australia
fact: Most of it is underground; the rock extends about 2.5 km beneath the surface.

title: Victoria Falls
hints: The largest sheet of falling water in the world
Locals call it 'the smoke that thunders'
David Livingstone named it after his queen in 1855
Its spray can be seen from 50 km away
On the Zambezi River
Found on the Zambia-Zimbabwe border
fact: At the edge sits the Devil's Pool, where swimmers lean over a 100 m drop in the dry season.

title: Mount Fuji
hints: A nearly perfect volcanic cone
Its country's highest peak at 3,776 m
Last erupted in 1707
Climbed by about 300,000 people each summer
Painted in a famous series of 36 views
Found on Honshu, Japan
fact: Women were banned from climbing it until 1872.

title: Great Barrier Reef
hints: The largest living structure on Earth
Visible from space
Made up of nearly 3,000 individual reefs
Home to 1,500 species of fish
Stretches 2,300 km along a coast
Found off Queensland, Australia
fact: Captain Cook ran aground on it in 1770 and spent seven weeks repairing his ship.

title: Iguazu Falls
hints: A chain of 275 waterfalls nearly 3 km wide
Its most dramatic drop is called the Devil's Throat
Eleanor Roosevelt reportedly exclaimed 'Poor Niagara!' on seeing it
Lies in subtropical rainforest
Straddles an international border
Found between Argentina and Brazil
fact: The name means 'big water' in the Guaraní language.

title: Mount Kilimanjaro
hints: The highest mountain in Africa at 5,895 m
A dormant volcano with three cones
The tallest free-standing mountain in the world
Its summit glaciers are rapidly disappearing
Rises alone above the savanna near Kenya
Found in Tanzania
fact: Climbers pass through five climate zones, from rainforest to arctic, on the way up.

title: Yellowstone (Old Faithful)
hints: The world's first national park, created in 1872
Sits atop a supervolcano
Contains half the world's geysers
Famous for a geyser that erupts roughly every 90 minutes
Wolves were reintroduced in 1995
Found mostly in Wyoming, USA
fact: The caldera is about 55 by 72 km across, far too large to see from the ground.

title: Hạ Long Bay
hints: A bay dotted with about 1,600 limestone islands
Its name means 'descending dragon'
Legend says a dragon spat out jewels that became the islands
Many islands are hollow with huge caves
On the Gulf of Tonkin
Found in northern Vietnam
fact: Some islands have floating fishing villages with their own schools.

title: Salar de Uyuni
hints: The largest salt flat in the world
After rain it becomes a giant mirror
Holds a large share of the world's lithium
So flat that satellites use it for calibration
At 3,650 m in the Andes
Found in Bolivia
fact: Hotels on the flat are built entirely from blocks of salt.

title: Dead Sea
hints: The lowest point on land, about 430 m below sea level
Nearly ten times saltier than the ocean
So dense that swimmers float effortlessly
Shrinking by about a metre a year
Bordered by Jordan, Israel, and the West Bank
Found in the Jordan Rift Valley
fact: Herod the Great used it as one of the world's first health resorts.

title: Matterhorn
hints: A pyramid-shaped peak with four distinct faces
Its first ascent in 1865 ended with four climbers falling to their deaths
Appears on a famous triangular chocolate bar
Stands above the car-free resort of Zermatt
On the Swiss-Italian border in the Alps
Found in Switzerland
fact: Each face points almost exactly to one of the compass directions.

title: Galápagos Islands
hints: A volcanic archipelago that inspired a theory of evolution
Home to giant tortoises and marine iguanas
Visited by Charles Darwin aboard HMS Beagle in 1835
Straddles the equator about 1,000 km offshore
Its name comes from the Spanish for tortoise
Found in the Pacific, part of Ecuador
fact: Lonesome George, the last of his subspecies, died here in 2012 at over 100 years old.

title: Serengeti
hints: A vast savanna famous for the Great Migration
Over a million wildebeest cross it every year
Its name means 'endless plains' in Maasai
Home to the largest lion population in Africa
Borders the Maasai Mara to the north
Found in northern Tanzania

title: Amazon River (Meeting of Waters)
hints: Where two rivers run side by side for 6 km without mixing
One is dark as tea, the other sandy brown
They differ in speed, temperature and acidity
The combined river is the largest in the world by volume
Beside a city with a famous opera house in the jungle
Found near Manaus, Brazil
fact: The Amazon discharges more water than the next seven largest rivers combined.

title: Sahara (Erg Chebbi)
hints: Towering orange sand dunes up to 150 m high
Part of the largest hot desert on Earth
Camel treks leave from a village called Merzouga
Night skies here are among the darkest anywhere
Near the Algerian border
Found in southeastern Morocco
fact: The wider desert is roughly the size of the United States.

title: Antelope Canyon
hints: A narrow slot canyon with wave-like sandstone walls
Carved by flash floods over millennia
Light beams pierce it at midday in summer
On Navajo Nation land
Near the town of Page and Lake Powell
Found in Arizona, USA
fact: Its Navajo name means 'the place where water runs through rocks'.

title: Zhangjiajie
hints: Thousands of towering sandstone pillars
Inspired the floating mountains in the film Avatar

Also home to a long glass-bottomed bridge
Its country's first national forest park
Found in Hunan, China

title: Plitvice Lakes
hints: Sixteen turquoise lakes connected by waterfalls
Natural travertine dams separate the lakes
Wooden boardwalks wind over the water
Its country's oldest and largest national park
In the Dinaric Alps
Found in Croatia

title: Cliffs of Moher
hints: Sea cliffs rising 214 m straight out of the Atlantic
Run for about 14 km along a coast
Home to 30,000 nesting seabirds including puffins
Appeared in Harry Potter and The Princess Bride
On the west coast of an island nation
Found in County Clare, Ireland

title: Great Blue Hole
hints: A giant circular sinkhole in the sea, 300 m across
Formed as a cave when sea levels were lower
Jacques Cousteau declared it a top dive site in 1971
Lies in the middle of a coral atoll
Off the coast of a Central American country
Found in Belize

title: Bora Bora
hints: A volcanic island ringed by a turquoise lagoon
Famous for overwater bungalows
Its twin peaks are the remains of an extinct volcano
Used as a US supply base in WWII
Part of the Society Islands
Found in French Polynesia

title: Giant's Causeway
hints: About 40,000 interlocking basalt columns
Formed by cooling lava 60 million years ago
Most columns are hexagonal
Legend says a giant built it to reach Scotland
On the north Antrim coast
Found in Northern Ireland

title: Pamukkale
hints: Dazzling white terraces of mineral pools on a hillside
Formed by calcium-rich hot springs
Its name means 'cotton castle'
The ancient spa city of Hierapolis sits on top
People have bathed here for 2,000 years
Found in southwestern Turkey

title: Denali
hints: The highest peak in North America at 6,190 m
Officially called Mount McKinley from 1917 to 2015
Its name means 'the high one' in Koyukon
Has a greater base-to-peak rise than Everest
Only visible on about 30% of summer days due to clouds
Found in Alaska, USA

title: Vatnajökull Glacier
hints: The largest glacier in Europe by volume
Covers about 8% of a country
Active volcanoes lie beneath the ice
Famous for blue ice caves in winter
Its meltwater feeds a lagoon of floating icebergs

title: Lake Baikal
hints: The deepest and oldest lake in the world

Home to the only freshwater seal species
Its ice is so clear and thick that cars drive across in winter
About 25 million years old
Found in Siberia, Russia

title: Komodo Island
hints: Home to the largest lizard in the world
Those lizards can grow to 3 m and weigh 70 kg
Also has a rare pink sand beach
Part of a national park with world-class diving
In the Lesser Sunda Islands
Found in Indonesia
fact: The dragons' bite delivers venom and bacteria; they can bring down a water buffalo.
